explanations.explanation: This neuron is a “label‐token” detector – it lights up on isolated metadata or heading-style subwords (month names in dates, single-letter or numeric identifiers, acronyms, domain fragments, Greek/technical parameters, etc.) that serve as structural labels or titles rather than running prose.

This feature fires on tokens that occur as standalone titles or section‐headers—often in title case or all-caps—marking the start of a new document block or headline (e.g. “BIO,” “Pin Ultimate,” “Buck Danny,” “company history,” etc.).
This neuron is basically a “subword-prefix” detector: it lights up on the initial piece of a word or token (acronym, compound stem or named-entity start) across languages and domains.
This feature flags the start of a document‐level heading or title (e.g. article headlines, section titles, episode names, patent titles, etc.) across diverse contexts.

explanations.explanation: This feature seems to fire on the little “linking” words that introduce the central math relation or operation in a problem statement—things like the preposition “of” in “probability of …,” the participle “picked” in “letters picked without replacement,” the noun “denominator” in “common denominator of …,” or even the Japanese conjunction および (“and”). In other words, it flags the functional token that ties the mathematical operator to its arguments.

This neuron specializes in “file-/module-level prologues” – the opening structural markers that kick off a document or compilation unit (e.g. import/includes/namespace lines, HTML/XML doctype or tags, license headers, top-level val/let/export bindings, IIFE headers, etc.). It flags tokens that introduce a new file or major section.

This feature fires on the very first, capitalized word of a heading or section title (e.g. PHP, Air, Brass, Military, Captain, Naval, Missile, President, Search, MIT, Russian, Student, About, Select), marking that token as the label of a new topic or subsection.

This feature consistently fires on the “last‐in‐a‐sequence” tokens across very different contexts—e.g. the final parameter in a function signature, the last `<enum>` in a styleable, the closing XML/HTML tag or attribute, the last element of an array or method‐chain call, even the trailing subword in an English contraction (’m, ’ve, ’re, ’d). In short, it marks boundary tokens that terminate a homogeneous list or chunk.

This neuron is a “boilerplate/structure” detector—it lights up on tokens that mark administrative or meta‐text rather than running prose.  In code it fires on the comment delimiters (e.g. */), in web and forum copy on site-owned phrases (“our … review,” “our cookie policy”), on negation cues in disclaimers (“no,” “don’t,” “do not”), and on section or category headings (“References,” “Category: Bacteria”), flagging UI/disclaimer/license/section-boundary language.

This neuron is basically a “dot‐boundary” detector – it fires on the period (or on tokens directly marking ends of sentences, abbreviations, version numbers, email addresses, section titles, etc.). In other words, it flags the punctuation or boundary marker that closes off a sentence, abbreviation, code/version string, domain name, heading, and so on.

This neuron fires on short, two‐token phrases that serve as structural labels or titles—everything from XML tag names (e.g. `<manifest>`) to blog/post headings and UI menu labels (“Main menu,” “Company history,” “Active Member,” etc.). It marks the start of a new section or prominent label in code or text.

This neuron fires on the “headline” or “topic” token in a span—i.e. the single content word (often a noun, proper name, acronym or key technical term) that names what the sentence, title or section is about. Examples include the main subject of a paper (ostomies, stents, cardiac recovery, vasopressin, GIST), a named entity or title (Hounds, Shade, Hareem Shah, Lido degli Estensi, Business Insider), Greek letters (β), counters or labels (篇, 枚, 回答), numerals (10), etc.

This neuron fires on structural “boundary” tokens that mark major block or section delimiters across both code and prose—things like comment- or doc-block openers (`/**`, `<?php`), license/header boilerplate, class/package declarations, section headings, and even sentence-final punctuation. It essentially flags where one high-level unit ends and the next begins.

This neuron fires on “structured” tokens in wiki‐style text—i.e. short alphanumeric chunks that serve as identifiers or measurements.  It lights up on pure numbers (years, page/file IDs, padded indices, coordinates, km→yd conversions), unit abbreviations following numbers (e.g. “kw”), and the little subword pieces that form proper names (e.g. “Eck,” “Lund”)—basically the bits of text that carry quantification or act as code‐like labels.

This feature lights up on the perfect‐aspect auxiliaries (especially “been” plus “has/have/we/it,” as in “has been shown,” “we have been asked,” “it has long been realized,” etc.), flagging constructions that background or report prior/still‐relevant states or events.

This feature fires on the kinds of high-level “heading” or metadata markers that kick off a new document or major section—e.g. standalone dates in news copy (“Yesterday”), all-caps labels (“UNPUBLISHED,” “TO BE PUBLISHED,” “RECORD IMPOUNDED”), court names and docket numbers in legal opinions, etc.

This neuron lights up on “boundary” markers in documents—things like sentence- or section-ending punctuation (e.g. a period at the end of a heading or sentence), blank-line breaks, and code comment delimiters—that signal the close or start of a structural block.

explanations.explanation: This feature flags indefinite quantifiers and hedge-style words in formal boilerplate (e.g. “any,” “some,” “those,” “pretty” as an intensifier) and related discourse markers that commonly occur in legal disclaimers, licensing notices, and academic prose.

1. Fires on the capital “F” at the start of “Finder” in multi‐word brand or service names.  
2. Activates on the noun “nail” when discussing manicure or nail‐art designs.  
3. Detects the prefix “Hor” of “horror” in contexts about horror films or threads.  
4. Recognizes the kanji fragment 映画大 (“movie-festival”) in Japanese film‐festival titles.  
5. Marks the acronym “DRM” denoting digital rights management for protected media.  
6. Captures the initial “Sp” of the TV show title “Spaced.”  
7. Identifies the token “beta” as the Greek letter/ordinal in set-theory notation.  
8. Fires on the prefix “Techn” in “technocracy,” the concept of technocratic governance.  
9. Activates on the prefix “Mov” in “movant,” the legal term for a party filing a motion.  
10. Detects the word “floor” when referring to building levels in real-estate listings.  
11. Marks the fragment “num” from the species epithet “numitor” in a butterfly’s Latin name.  
12. Fires on the fragment “tub” in “tubules,” referring to microscopic anatomical structures.  
13. Recognizes the word “inclusion” in the phrase “inclusion cysts” in ovarian pathology.  
14. Activates on “escape” in the compound “escape room” for puzzle‐based games.  
15. Captures the phrase “Credit Repair” in listings of financial repair services.  
16. Detects the prefix “Sh” in the title “Throwing Shade,” the name of a talk show.

This feature fires on structural-boundary markers in text and code—e.g. blank lines or line breaks separating paragraphs or sections, heading/title lines at the top of a block, and comment delimiters (/* … */) in code. It’s essentially detecting “section separators.”

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on word-initial morphemes—that is, common subword prefixes (e.g. the Semitic definite articles ה/ال, Greek/Latin technical prefixes like hydro-/thermo-/ultra-/lympho-/amphio-/arterio-, etc.) across languages and domains.

This neuron lights up on text-structure boundaries – it peaks on punctuation used as separators (commas, hyphens, pipes and dash runs in ASCII art or code comments) and on the first subword of a new segment (e.g. the “w” in “-worn,” “woken,” “wistful,” or “sp” in “spinner”/“spiele”).

This neuron fires on the final token of a news‐style headline or section label—i.e. the punctuation or last word that marks the end of a title/tag (like “In Plain English,” “CinemaNow,” “Insurance enrollment,” “News,” “Inc.,” etc.) and signals the transition into the body text.

This neuron fires on isolated, atomic subword tokens—especially single‐character bits like digits, lone letters or Greek symbols, punctuation marks, and one‐char graphemes—regardless of language or context.
This feature fires on the opening subtoken of a capitalized label—whether a speaker name, article heading, section title or proper‐noun—marking the start of a new titled or named chunk.

This feature isn’t really about “Excel” or “time arithmetic” or “Russian,” but about spotting rare or unusual subword tokens.  It tends to peak on things like two-digit numbers (49, 50, 51, 0040, etc.), odd HTML/JSON IDs, Cyrillic fragments (ком, сер­в, щен…), even unusual English chunks (minimal, a lone “V”), i.e. low-frequency pieces that stand out against the model’s common vocabulary.
This feature detects Markdown-style “strong” emphasis markers (the double-asterisks **…**) that surround headings, titles or other bolded labels in the text.

This neuron detects short character-sequence “chunks” – roots, affixes or abbreviations of about 2–4 letters – that recur in specialized vocabulary (e.g. surgical suffixes like –ostomy, tumor-type stems (schwann–), enzyme or hematology roots (HDC, hemat–), cardinal names (beth), system or brand names (Health), Greek/Latin prefixes (G in GIST) and even isolated symbols or numbers, across diverse technical, biomedical and mathematical texts.

This neuron is essentially flagging the “meaty” root or initial subword of content-heavy words (often technical terms, proper nouns or specialized vocabulary). It acts like a prefix/morpheme detector that lights up on the first chunk of important domain-specific words across a wide range of contexts.

This neuron flags words and short phrases used as section headings, link/CTA labels or other UI metadata in web‐style documents (e.g. “Register Now,” “Cookie Policy,” “Field,” “Transport Time,” “Top 10,” etc.).

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on the token that closes out a top‐level line or block—i.e. the final keyword, symbol or punctuation marking the end of a standalone directive/import/comment/heading/title/sentence across code, markup and prose.
This feature detects the standard scientific “n = …” sample‐size notation—i.e. the token “n” (and nearby markers) used across clinical/biological papers to indicate group or subject counts.
This feature is a detector for the “.” full-stop token—i.e. the period punctuation marking ends of sentences or common abbreviations in formal/legal/technical text.

This neuron flags the little “hinge” words that launch caveats or open‐ended lists in legal or advisory text—contrastive/limiting connectives like “but,” “without,” “not,” “at” in phrases such as “but not limited to,” “including without limitation,” or “at your own risk.”

This neuron fires on standalone, capitalized labels and headings—things like menu/navigation items, section titles or UI call-to-actions (e.g. “Main menu,” “Send,” “News,” “Trip,” “Navigation,” etc.).

This neuron fires on the “head” or first chunk of structured, domain-specific tokens—whether that’s a month name in a date (Feb, Jun, February), a numeric or Greek index (2, 4, β), an acronym initial (G in GIST, m in Mootools), or the key root/morpheme of a technical term (sulf- in sulfotransferase, oph- in dermatophytes, om- in ostomies, am- in amiloride, circum- in circumscripta, inclusion in inclusion cysts).

This feature fires on the “preamble” or header tokens that identify a document’s context via standardized metadata markers—things like docket numbers and court names in legal filings, copyright/license comment blocks, “use strict” and module/controller definitions in scripts, and package/import/using-namespace declarations in code.

This feature marks “ending” pieces in structured sequences or compounds—whether it’s the final number in a parenthesized list (years, patent‐ID or RGBA values), the last subtoken of a hyphen/underscore-joined identifier or unit (PLE in COU-PLE, dp, ICC, ier in multiplier), or the closing ordinal/discourse word that caps off a phrase (première, furthermore, yet, way).
This neuron is simply picking up the two‐letter sequence “ar” (in any casing) as a subword unit, regardless of the surrounding language or domain.

This neuron is picking up document‐structure boundaries—i.e. the tokens that start or end headlines, section titles, bylines and dateline abbreviations (e.g. “Rep.,” “U.S.,” “N.Y.”), file-type labels (“PDF”), author names and the final word of a heading. It marks the margins of content blocks rather than ordinary sentence tokens.
